problems.description: SonarQube cognitive complexity +23 for only +15 lines — inline validation branching in add_task/edit_task could be extracted into a small validation helper to keep route handlers flat.
Moving init_db() to module level runs schema DDL as an import side effect; correct for WSGI but can surprise tests/imports. Consider an app factory or lazy init pattern if the codebase grows.

Convention score 0.71 is driven by 8 violations (PascalCase/snake_case) all located in files NOT touched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) — pre-existing repo debt, not introduced here. Flagging as discrepancy: the diff itself is convention-clean.

strengths: Fixes a real logic bug: default task status changed from 'done' to 'pending'
Removes dead code (_legacy_format_date helper, _notify_admin stub) without changing behavior
Adds proper input validation: type checks for title/status and non-empty title guard on POST and PUT
Deduplicates the redundant init_db() call that ran both at import and in __main__
Zero new files/functions/classes — changes stay contained within the existing single-file structure
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-respecting bugfix+hardening commit (correct default status, dead-code removal, input validation) whose low convention score is purely pre-existing debt in untouched files, offset by a minor complexity bump from inline validation branching.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' constant, shipping with a predictable signing key if env is unset; should fail closed or require the env var.
Auth endpoints have no rate limiting or account-lockout, leaving /auth/login and /auth/register open to brute-force attacks.
update_task builds conditional WHERE clauses and params imperatively; adding the owner_id branch grows the existing f-string SQL pattern into more complex, harder-to-read code.
Input-validation and error-response logic is duplicated between register() and login(); a shared helper would reduce the +16 new functions' maintenance surface.
Uses deprecated datetime.utcnow(), which is removed in Python 3.12; should use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Auth concerns (tokens, decorators, user CRUD) are embedded in the single app.py module; acceptable given the existing single-file structure but increases module cohesion risk as the app grows.

strengths: Schema migration uses PRAGMA table_info to add owner_id via ALTER TABLE, keeping databases created under the previous schema usable without dropping rows.
Reuses existing get_db()/init_db() helpers and the established snake_case + type-hinted signature style rather than introducing new patterns.
Per-owner scoping is applied consistently via g.user and parameterized SQL (bound params, injection-safe) across list/get/update paths.
Auth decorator and token helpers are small, focused, and error paths return consistent JSON error envelopes matching existing route responses.
commit_reviews.summary: Cohesive feature_addition session that adds JWT auth and per-owner task scoping while cleanly preserving existing patterns and data, though a hardcoded secret fallback and duplicated validation logic introduce modest security/maintainability debt.

problems.description: The synchronous API path (PUT /tasks/<id>) now depends on the Celery broker: .delay() publishes to Redis inline, so a down broker fails the request, while a live broker with no worker silently drops the notification (the mock email is just a print).

Over-engineering: a full Celery app with broker_url, result_backend, and a dedicated 'notifications' queue is introduced to mock an email that only prints; a lightweight in-process task would match the story's scope.
Semantic naming mismatch: owner['username'] is passed as the user_email parameter of send_notification_email.

New files add convention violations (7 new smells, convention score 0.71); celery_config.py and tasks.py trigger PascalCase/UPPER_CASE flags, though several reported violations are in untouched files (repositories.py, test_app.py) and are pre-existing/false positives.
Introduces new runtime dependencies (celery, redis) with no visible requirement/lockfile change in the diff.
Tests monkeypatch app.send_notification_email.delay, so the real task and broker path are never exercised; there is no coverage of the worker or broker-down scenario.

strengths: Notification is correctly gated on the status transition to 'completed' (current_task vs updated task), preventing duplicate sends on re-edits.
Tests cover both the happy path and the no-duplicate-notification edge case.
Reuses existing patterns (get_task, get_db, g.user) and keeps new config isolated in celery_config.py with env-var overrides.
commit_reviews.summary: The commit integrates an async notification feature that reuses existing route patterns and has solid transition-gating logic and tests, but it over-weights a mock email with real Celery/Redis infrastructure and couples the API path to broker availability, leaving the measured 0.71 convention score as the main compliance concern.

problems.description: TaskRepository/UserRepository are instantiated on every call (e.g. TaskRepository(get_db) in each route); the factory pattern would be cleaner with module-level instances or a single injected factory.

repositories.py introduces a new module-level constant violation: ConnectionFactory type alias is lowercase, which the convention checker flags as requiring UPPER_CASE (or TypeAlias/PascalCase per Python typing conventions).

Repository methods use closing(self.connection_factory()) without an explicit commit in the visible portion of the diff; the original code relied on `with get_db() as conn` + conn.commit(), so transaction/commit semantics should be verified as preserved.

strengths: Extracts SQL into a clean repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), removing ~92 lines of duplicated inline queries from app.py
Centralizes schema creation in initialize_database(), improving the previous ALTER TABLE migration approach
SonarQube delta confirms net improvement: -3 smells, -4 cognitive complexity, +0 bugs, +0 duplications
Preserves the public function API and route behavior in app.py, keeping the refactor low-risk
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped repository-pattern refactor that reduces duplication and complexity with no new bugs, held back only by a minor convention slip in the new file's type alias.

problems.description: paginate_tasks() returns limit+1 rows: the next-page sentinel row leaks across the repository boundary, forcing the route in app.py:157-158 to re-slice (tasks[:limit]) to reconstruct the page. The method contract should return exactly `limit` rows plus a has_more flag, or document the sentinel.

Duplicate filter/WHERE building in paginate_tasks(): the owner_id filter, params, and WHERE string assembly are copied between the COUNT query and the data query (repositories.py:102-118), which will drift if filters change.

rate_limit_key() decodes the JWT on every request, duplicating the decode require_auth already performs when it populates g.user. This is redundant work per request and duplicates the auth/trust boundary.

list_tasks() grew +34 cognitive complexity (measured): inline parsing, range validation, sentinel slicing, and envelope assembly all live in the route. Extracting a validation helper or an envelope builder would flatten the branching.

Measured convention score is 0.71 with 8 violations (app.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, celery_config.py, test_app.py). All 8 are in files/functions untouched by this commit (celery_config.py and tasks.py date from session 3); the commit's own additions are snake_case, type-hinted, and docstringed. Discrepancy: the 0.71 is cumulative repo debt, not introduced here.

GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare list to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking consumer contract. Internally consistent (all tests updated) and reasonable for pagination, but unannounced.

strengths: Cursor pagination is implemented as a proper keyset query (ORDER BY id DESC, id < cursor, LIMIT limit+1) in TaskRepository, correctly respecting the session-4 repository pattern rather than duplicating SQL in the route.

Rate limiting uses Flask-Limiter with per-user keys (JWT sub) and client-IP fallback, Redis storage with in-memory fallback enabled — production-appropriate and consistent with the existing Redis integration from session 3.

Solid test coverage: pagination page boundaries and terminal page, cursor/limit validation errors, the 100/min boundary plus a 429 with Retry-After header, and app.limiter.reset() in the fixture to isolate tests.
Measured delta is clean: 0 new bugs and -6 code smells, indicating the change reduces static-analysis debt while adding features.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted cross-cutting change — rate limiting and cursor pagination slotted into the existing repository/route architecture with strong tests and a clean measured delta — marred only by minor debt (sentinel-row leak across the repository boundary, duplicated WHERE building, and a redundant JWT decode in the rate-limit key function).

compounding_issues: No requirements.txt until Session 5 — Flask, PyJWT, celery, redis, and flask-limiter were used across Sessions 2-4 with no dependency manifest, so the project was unreproducible for most of the story
Dead 'legacy' cruft persisted: the fetch_task alias and fetch_task/get_task duplication survived all refactors, and the JWT_SECRET development default was never hardened
Session 2's ALTER TABLE schema migration (adding owner_id) became a permanent load-time cost and complexity that every later session had to carry forward into repositories.py
key_decisions: Session 1: fix the seed's status bug (INSERT 'done' vs return 'pending'), move init_db to module load, and add input validation — establishing correctness before features
Session 2: JWT auth + users table with owner_id and an idempotent ALTER TABLE migration — per-user data isolation became the foundation all later features rely on
Session 3: Celery async notification on the pending→completed transition, isolated in celery_config.py + tasks.py rather than inlining in the route
Session 4: extract a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC, TaskRepository, UserRepository) with connection-factory injection — a behavior-preserving refactor that slims app.py and enables Session 5
Session 5: cursor-based id pagination plus Flask-Limiter keyed by JWT subject/IP as cross-cutting concerns, and finally adding the dependency manifest
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the story. Session 1 repaired seeded defects and added validation; Session 2 added a substantial auth feature with the first real test suite; Session 3 integrated asynchronous notifications with transition-guard tests; Session 4 was a clean, behavior-preserving refactor into a repository layer with the existing tests staying green; and Session 5 layered pagination and rate limiting on top while expanding tests to cover them. The code moved from a buggy 146-line single-file app to a structured, multi-module, 10-test API, with the one persistent wart being the missing dependency manifest until the final session.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent story where each session builds naturally on the prior — bug fixes, then auth, async integration, a structural refactor, and cross-cutting hardening — with quality improving throughout and only minor compounding debt (a late dependency manifest and lingering legacy aliases).
